vignette: The accident happens on a Tuesday, on a stretch of coastal highway his Oceania family has driven for generations. He is sixty-three, married to Elena for thirty-two years, and works as a financial analyst who spent three decades modeling uncertainty. He trusts the math. He trusts the margins. One moment he is merging, the next, a delivery truck runs the red light. The world folds inward. Glass rains into his lap. The engine dies. Silence, thick and absolute, presses against his eardrums. When the paramedics cut him out, he counts his breaths. One, two, three. Each feels borrowed. The impact leaves no wound on his skin, but it hollows out the floor beneath him. In the weeks that follow, he tries to return to his desk. He opens his quarterly forecasts and sees only gaps, blank cells where certainty used to live. His mind, trained to balance ledgers, tries to calculate the probability of survival, but the equation keeps resetting. He tells himself he is fine. He sits in his office, staring at risk matrices that no longer look like tools, only warnings. He begins to leave at noon, then takes unpaid leave. His colleagues mistake his withdrawal for burnout. He does not correct them. Home becomes a place of quiet surveillance. He measures the distance between his car and the garage door. He buys groceries in daylight. He refuses to drive after dark. "The headlights blind you," he tells Elena, not looking at her. She notices the way he flinches when he hears a hard brake from the street below. She finds him standing in the kitchen at 2 a.m., checking the deadbolt for the fourth time, his breath shallow, his shoulders locked. He tells her he is fine, but his voice is too steady, too quiet, the kind of calm that comes from shutting doors. At work, his reports have grown so conservative, so cautious, that his managing partner asks for a meeting. He tells them he is recalibrating. What he does not say is that he can no longer distinguish between plausible risk and inevitability. Every spreadsheet feels like a bet with a loaded die. His analysis, once sharp, now hovers at the edges of possibility, paralyzed by the ghost of a single Tuesday. He misses the old version of himself-the one who could forecast a merger without checking the sky for storms. Sleep becomes a negotiation. He lies awake, listening to the house settle, convinced he hears the crumple of metal, the hiss of airbags, the radio static before the first siren. When he dreams, he wakes with his heart hammering against his ribs, his sheets tangled around his legs like tangled seatbelts. Elena rests her hand on his back, and he tenses, then slowly unclenches. He measures everything in margins of safety, in buffer zones, in the quiet terror of losing control. In session, he speaks in careful increments. He describes the weight of a coffee cup, the texture of the armchair, the exact shade of gray in the storm clouds that day. He does not cry. He does not need to. His body remembers what his words hold back. The car sits in the driveway, untouched, its windshield still faintly cracked at the corner. He will sell it eventually, he says, when the timing is right. He has not yet found the right time.
